question_text: Explain which pre-bottling treatments and QC analyses you would consider most important for an inexpensive, organic, vegan wine.
command_word_demand: This question required candidates to think about implications of the specified parameters, i.e. explain choices as they follow from the combination of inexpensive + organic + vegan, not general QC knowledge.

definitions_required.quote: An inexpensive wine should have been defined. Markets do vary, but a 20 Euro wine is hardly inexpensive for most.

required_elements.element: Treat the question as one single wine with all three parameters (inexpensive, organic, vegan) combined, not three separate wines
required_elements.quote: Most candidates did understand that the question was meant to cover one wine with all these parameters, but some considered three different wines.

required_elements.element: Know which additives/treatments are prohibited under organic regulation (e.g. no electrodialysis, reverse osmosis) and avoid proposing them
required_elements.quote: Awareness of legislation for organic wine - must comply with EU or other applicable rules which specifies permitted additives and processing techniques (e.g. no electrodialysis, reverse osmosis etc). ... Many answers were let down by lack of awareness of permitted additives and treatments under organic regulations - so proposing electrodialysis, CMC, sorbic acid, PVPP or Velcorin were errors.

required_elements.element: Know permitted sulphite levels for organic wine (lower than non-organic) for at least EU and other key markets like USA
required_elements.quote: Lower sulphite levels than non-organic wine. ... Knowledge of permitted sulphite levels, at least for EU and other key markets like USA, was required.

required_elements.element: Correctly distinguish sulphur from sulphite (not use interchangeably)
required_elements.quote: Once again, some candidates used sulphur and sulphite as interchangeable, which is incorrect.

required_elements.element: Explain that vegan means no animal-derived products even as processing aids (not just ingredients), with implications for traceability and choice of fining agents
required_elements.quote: A number of candidates were not aware of what vegan meant - it's not just about ingredients but also any animal derived products as processing aids even if not detectable in the final wine. This has implications for traceability at all stages and limits the range of fining products that can be used.

required_elements.element: Recognise the production pressures of an inexpensive wine: high volume, quicker throughput (no time for barrels, natural clarification etc.), need for stability, clarity, freedom from hazes/deposits, possible residual sugar
required_elements.quote: Awareness of production pressures of inexpensive wine - likely to be high volume, quicker winery throughput (no time for barrels, natural clarification etc). ... It was also reasonable to expect that an inexpensive wine needed to be stable, clear, free from hazes and deposits and possibly would contain residual sugar, and would likely need to be prepared quickly and in large volumes.

required_elements.element: Use price-appropriate examples, not premium wines
required_elements.quote: It was not helpful to use examples of premium wines such as classed growth Bordeaux or Ridge to illustrate this answer.

credit_signals.signal: Discussed implications of reduced protection at lower SO2 levels and the need for hygiene, filtration and pH management
credit_signals.quote: Good candidates discussed the implications of reduced protection at lower SO2 levels and the need to pay attention to hygiene, filtration and pH management.

penalty_signals.signal: Wrote general QC answers rather than answers tailored to the question's specific parameters
penalty_signals.quote: Candidates writing poor answers lacked factual knowledge and tended to write general QC answers rather than thinking about the question

penalty_signals.signal: Wasted time covering earlier stages of the winemaking process instead of pre-bottling treatments/QC
penalty_signals.quote: in some cases, time was wasted covering earlier parts of the winemaking process

scope_traps.trap: Treating the question as covering three separate wines (one inexpensive, one organic, one vegan) instead of a single wine combining all three parameters
Illustrating an 'inexpensive' wine with premium examples
scope_traps.quote: It was not helpful to use examples of premium wines such as classed growth Bordeaux or Ridge to illustrate this answer.

question_text: What steps should a winemaker take, in preparation for bottling and at bottling, to prevent microbial spoilage? Consider both red and white wines.
command_word_demand: "a technical question requires a technical answer" — candidates needed to give specific, technical, numeric answers (e.g. actual SO2 levels), not general commentary on microbial spoilage.

definitions_required.quote: This question required a definition of microbial spoilage. Microbiological spoilage organisms can be any which are unwanted at a particular stage (but typically bacteria and yeast)...

required_elements.element: Define microbial spoilage precisely, including that cork taint is not microbial spoilage
required_elements.quote: This question required a definition of microbial spoilage. ... Cork taint is not considered microbial spoilage.

required_elements.element: Distinguish the differing risks for red versus white wines, primarily because red wines have no/very low malic acid and are usually fermented dry
required_elements.quote: The risks differ for red and white wines primarily because red wines have no/very low levels of malic acid and are usually fermented dry.

required_elements.element: State the correct free SO2 range at bottling (25-35mg/L or 0.8ppm molecular, up to 40mg/L for special cases like bulk or dessert wines) and not confuse free/total/molecular SO2
required_elements.quote: In very simple terms, free sulphur dioxide levels at bottling should be between 25 - 35mg/L or 0.8ppm molecular. Special cases e.g. bulk wines or dessert wines may go up to 40mg/L. It is of great concern that 56 candidates, or 65% of all that answered this question, either provided levels outside this range, didn't mention any level or discussed total sulphur dioxide as the preventative level for microbial spoilage.

required_elements.element: Show that prevention (hygiene, filtration, gas management, temperature control) is the primary strategy, not treatments/additives applied just prior to bottling
required_elements.quote: Prevention is better than cure. In many situations cure is not possible. Hygiene is the number one rule in preventing microbial spoilage. ... Trying to fix, in the case of this topic, microbial spoilage just prior to bottling is near impossible and candidates didn't grasp this.

required_elements.element: Correctly distinguish VA/Brettanomyces/other spoilage organisms rather than confusing VA with Acetobacter
required_elements.quote: confusing VA with Acetobacter

required_elements.element: Cover hygiene, gas management and temperature control, not just SO2 management
required_elements.quote: confining the answer to SO2 management; lack of coverage of hygiene, gas management and temperature control

penalty_signals.signal: Wrote about microbial spoilage in general without defining major risks and implications, resulting in superficial answers
penalty_signals.quote: It was much harder to write a well-structured essay without defining the major risks and implications and many candidates simply wrote about microbial spoilage in general, which tended to result in superficial answers.

penalty_signals.signal: Confused free, total and molecular SO2
penalty_signals.quote: Particular weaknesses noted included confusing free, total and molecular SO2; errors on filtering and pore sizes

penalty_signals.signal: Implied chemical processes (DMDC, sorbic acid, velcorin, lysozyme, chitosan) applied at bottling are normal practice, rather than describing remedial steps prior to that point
penalty_signals.quote: A considerable number of candidates implied that applying these and other additives at the time of bottling was normal practice rather than showing/explaining remedial steps and processes prior to getting it to this point.

penalty_signals.signal: Assumed big wineries need more rigorous bottling hygiene than small wineries
penalty_signals.quote: Some candidates clearly felt that big wineries/facilities need to have a more rigorous bottling hygiene/cleaning regime than small wineries/facilities.

performance_note: 65% of the 86 candidates who answered this question either gave free SO2 levels outside the correct range, didn't mention any level, or discussed total SO2 instead of free SO2.

question_text: Describe a comprehensive QA and QC system a large winery should implement for the management of dry goods.
command_word_demand: A comprehensive description of a QA/QC system, requiring clear practical knowledge and good examples, not a discussion of procurement or supply management (which the report treats as out of scope).

definitions_required.quote: This answer required a definition of QA/QC.

It also required a definition of dry goods, which should include all packaging goods (bottle, cask or any other vessel, closure, cartons, dividers and labels) plus any products used in the winemaking e.g. yeast, enzyme, tartaric acid, fining agents and oak barrels.

required_elements.element: Define QA/QC and define dry goods (packaging goods plus winemaking inputs like yeast, enzyme, tartaric acid, fining agents, oak barrels)
required_elements.quote: This answer required a definition of QA/QC. It also required a definition of dry goods, which should include all packaging goods (bottle, cask or any other vessel, closure, cartons, dividers and labels) plus any products used in the winemaking e.g. yeast, enzyme, tartaric acid, fining agents and oak barrels.

required_elements.element: Describe a full written procedure so all winery departments understand the process, covering receipt, storage and use of dry goods, with awareness that wine is a food product and consumer safety is paramount
required_elements.quote: A full written procedure is put in place so all departments at the winery understand the process to ensure dry goods are received, stored and utilised to enable a wine to be produced, bottled and stored in the correct and safe manner, being aware that wine is a food product and consumer safety is paramount.

required_elements.element: Include flow diagrams, HACCP, ability to pass an annual supplier audit, and adequate records for an annual external audit (e.g. BRC)
required_elements.quote: A QA/QC system must include flow diagrams, HACCP and be able to pass an annual supplier audit and with adequate records for an annual external audit like British Retail Consortium (BRC) or other audits.

required_elements.element: Address storage conditions to avoid damage or contamination of dry goods, and that dry goods must match brand specifications
required_elements.quote: Dry goods must also match any brand specifications. ... Storage conditions should also be considered, to avoid damage or contamination.

credit_signals.signal: Showed clear practical knowledge and offered good examples
credit_signals.quote: good answers showed clear practical knowledge and offered good examples

penalty_signals.signal: Wasted time discussing procurement procedures or supply management, which are distinct from QA/QC systems
penalty_signals.quote: Some candidates wasted too much time discussing procurement procedures or managing supply of goods which are distinct from QA/QC systems.

penalty_signals.signal: Did not cover sufficient ground
penalty_signals.quote: Weak answers just did not cover sufficient ground.

examples_expected.quote: and with adequate records for an annual external audit like British Retail Consortium (BRC) or other audits

scope_traps.trap: Discussing procurement/supply management instead of the QA/QC system itself
scope_traps.quote: Some candidates wasted too much time discussing procurement procedures or managing supply of goods which are distinct from QA/QC systems.

performance_note: Not many candidates tackled this question.

question_text:
What are the key factors to consider in drawing up a technical specification for:

a. a white dessert wine bottled at source with 150g/l of residual sugar; and
b. an entry-level red wine imported in bulk with 4g/l of residual sugar
command_word_demand: Identify what needs to be in a technical specification and why, for each of the two named wine scenarios - not a general discussion of quality control or a list of wine treatments.

required_elements.element: Show that the key objective of a technical specification is to ensure the wine arrives with the importer in good quality and chemically stable condition, for sale (white, bottled at source) or for final treatment prior to bottling (red, bulk)
required_elements.quote: Candidates should show understanding that the key objective of technical specifications is to ensure wines arrive with the importer in a good quality and chemically stable condition for sale to the consumer (white) or for final treatment prior to bottling (red).

required_elements.element: Highlight the potential spoilage risks specific to each style: a very sweet wine and a dry red wine
required_elements.quote: Should also highlight the potential spoilage which may arise in a very sweet wine and in a dry red wine.

required_elements.element: Understand what a typical specification covers and the differences between a bottled specification and a bulk one
required_elements.quote: Should also understand what a typical specification should cover. There will be differences between a bottled specification and a bulk one.

required_elements.element: Address implications and risks specific to the wine styles and likely price points, e.g. the high residual sugar level, and treatments required for bottled-at-source vs bulk-shipped-then-bottled wines
required_elements.quote: What are the implications and risks for those specific wine styles (high level of residual sugar etc.) and likely price points? ... Highlight what treatments are required for a wine bottled at source and then shipped in bottle and a wine shipped in bulk and prepared for bottling at destination.

credit_signals.quote: Good answers included factual and practical detail.

penalty_signals.signal: Talked about quality control in general or offered a list of wine treatments rather than considering what needs to be in a specification and why
penalty_signals.quote: Weak answers again talked about quality control in general or offered a list of wine treatments rather than considering what needs to be in a specification and why.

scope_traps.trap: Assuming a technical specification is always necessary regardless of volume/premium status
scope_traps.quote: Note that many purchasers may not even consider a technical specification necessary for smaller volumes of a (likely) premium sweet wine bottled at source.

performance_note: This was not a popular question but should have been straightforward as it was quite simply about product specifications.
